incident_description: I was a 49 year old female who purchased a Hairstreaq Detangling Hairbrush through Amazon online. The Hairbrush was in a two-pack and each was identical except for the brush's color. I used the same brush for about three months, approximately 4 times per day. At first it seemed fine, but gradually over time I started experiencing balance issues, then increased headaches. In the last two weeks of using the brush I started to feel my vision being disturbed and my headaches increased dramatically, as well as a fall. Near the end of June, 2024, I accidentally placed the hairbrush near a metal paperclip and it jumped from a short distance to the handle of the brush. I then discovered the hairbrush had a strong magnet inside the handle. I immediately stopped using the brushes and threw them away, but my symptoms were getting worse over the next few days. I went to a doctor and requested a Brain CT scan because I was fearful of my brain being injured. I have two brain shunts in my brain. These have programmable valves in the brain shunts. I have had many shunts implanted because of a childhood diagnosis of hydrocephalus. I have been informed for many years to avoid magnets near my head where the shunts are placed, including magnetic scanners and cell phones near my head because of the danger that magnets might cause to the shunt settings. On July 2, 2024 it was determined I had pressure on the brain. On July 4th, 2024 I was admitted through the Emergency Department for possible brain shunt surgery. That is when I told the neurosurgical resident about my discovery a few days before of the magnet in the brush handle being there without my knowledge, which I had been using for three months. I was sent for further imaging and it was determined that my shunt settings had changed from their original settings to incorrect settings that caused neurological symptoms from cerebrospinal fluid imbalance, which caused my brain to swell. Instead of surgery, they reset my valve settings externally to the correct settings with subsequent resolution of symptoms. My research shows that about 200,000 people are implanted each year with magnet-sensitive devices in the heart, head, and other areas, which could disrupt the device. There was no notice, warning, instructions, or labels on the hair brush or the inner or outer packaging that could let a consumer know of this danger of this product. A simple warning that the handle contained a magnet would have probably been enough to prevent this injury.
justification: The incident resulted in injury, as evidenced by the person's symptoms and required medical intervention to correct shunt settings. The likelihood of occurrence is classified as possible due to the specific conditions required for a similar incident to happen.

incident_description:

About 20 minutes later, while sitting a few feet away, I heard an extremely loud bang as the battery exploded. Smoke began pouring out of the device. I quickly unplugged it from the electrical wall outlet and opened a window.
A few minutes later, while assessing the situation, there was a secondary explosion. Thick white and gray smoke filled the room, and black ashes emerged from the battery compartment of the massage gun. I retrieved a fire extinguisher and monitored the situation. Fortunately, there were no flames, and I was able to remove the massage gun from my house using gloves and placing it in a box. In hindsight, I should have called the fire department, but everything happened so quickly.
It took 12 hours with all windows open and fans on to clear the chemical smoke. The incident contaminated nearby linens and left scorch marks on the table, along with black soot surrounding the area.
Fortunately, I was sitting far enough away when it occurred that I was uninjured, and it was on a fire-resistant surface. If I had been holding it, I could have been seriously injured, and if it had been on a different surface, it might have resulted in a fire. Im also grateful that I was home when it happened; if it had occurred while I was away, my pets could have been at risk of chemical smoke inhalation and poisoning, in addition to the risk of a house fire.
Im also relieved that I didnt try to remove it from the house after the first explosion, as I could have been injured during the secondary explosion. The incident was very frightening, and Im fortunate that circumstances prevented injury or serious damage.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage and contamination but no injury or death occurred. The likelihood of such an event is considered rare given the specific circumstances described.

incident_description:
MANSCAPED sells The Handyman Compact Face Shaver.
It is described as "Portable Mens Travel Facial Hair Groomer, USB-C Rechargeable Electric Razor, Waterproof, Cordless, Dual-Action SkinSafe Long-Hair Leveler & Foil Blades".
It is available not only alone, but as a bundle kit other accessories in different combo models.

This device almost caught fire or did catch fire in a smoldering manner, releasing toxic plastic fumes throughout the home to which people were exposed. A fire was very possible if there was any combustible material nearby, especially if the would-be-fire had not been caught early by someone with a good sense of smell. Those who are not able to locate or infer the sources of smells may be more at risk of death, property damage, or homelessness by fire.

The product comprises a USB-C charging cable, USB-C male charger wall outlet adapter, and the handheld product itself comprising of a grippable rechargeable battery sub-unit (and a cutter-and-foil-shaver sub-unit). While charging with the provided adapter (which has the same voltage and current markings as the battery unit), the battery unit overheated drastically, and over the course of half an hour leaked plastic fumes throughout the building. The product had disintegrated and melted on the battery unit where the USB-C cable connects to the charging circuitry. Charging port had reached sufficient heat that the plastic had melted onto the cable. At this temperature, we do not know if the lithium ion batteries may have been at risk themselves of catching fire.

A previous purchase of this product had sporadically-malfunctioning charging, so one can only surmise that the issue is systemic with this model, and perhaps with the manufacturer that MANSCAPED is working with in China, and related charging circuitry of related products.
justification: The incident involved a product malfunction that released toxic fumes but did not result in injury or death. The likelihood of occurrence is considered possible given the description of a previous purchase with similar malfunctioning charging issues.

incident_description:
I'm writing regarding the APOKE 3 in 1 Hair Dryer Brush & Straightener Brush on Amazon at [REDACTED].

This product is a fire/burn hazard and claims UL certification when I don't believe it's actually certified. I use this product to blow dry and straighten my hair at the same time (reduces frizziness). I have not experienced any fire or injuries.

I am copy/pasting my [REDACTED] below.
---
Lot of twists and turns here, so bear with me!

Original review: Great product, I wish a reliable company made it. Used it twice, then I kept hearing a staticky sound. I believe it has a short in it. I was already on the fence because this is an unknown brand and there is NO thingy on the end of the cord. The sound only happens when I plug it in, so in the trash it goes.

UPDATE: I was sent a replacement...which is clearly used. It was not in the wrapper, and the cords did not have twist ties (the cord was sort of wrapped around the barrel). Ew.

UPDATE UPDATE: I was asked by the company if I used the used one, and if so, did it work? Who uses a used beauty product?! That's disgusting, and I told them this. They sent a replacement...which also makes the staticky sound.

UPDATE UPDATE UPDATE: The sparking sound defect is happening in the replacement's replacement. I know what's going on. It's related to something I mentioned in the original review because I thought it very strange when I pulled the dryer out of the box. If you look, you'll notice it, too.

*This hair dryer has no external ALCI.* ALCI stands for Appliance Leakage Circuit Interrupter, and it's what saves lives when an appliance is dropped in water for example. It's the little box on the plug with the "test" and "reset" buttons! It senses a problem with the circuit - moisture, a fault in the product, or a fault with the outlet - and shuts off the product. This dryer does not have the UL symbol because UL requires *all* hair dryers to have an ALCI to obtain certification.

This is why the dryer makes the staticky/sparking sound (like static electricity discharging) or just stops working. It has a fault, and when it recognizes it and shuts off, you can't push the little button and reset it yourself. On functional versions of this product, you may be fine the first 24 power cycles or so, but then you'll hear the staticky sound and a click not long after that. The sound stops after the click. That's the internal mechanism doing its job. Sometimes the product shuts off and does *not* fix itself, but that's somebody else's review.

On my first dryer, there was no click, ever. I'd plug it back in, the sparking sound began again. On the replacement, the click worked correctly. I'd plug it back in, and no sparking sound. This is supposed to happen every time, but it doesn't.

This is why *external* ALCIs are the norm.

This company (or its supplier) tried to cut costs, and they're gonna burn down your house instead. They made a defective product and put in their own defective safeguards to stop you from noticing until you are outside of the 90 day return window. Or they made a product to sell cheaply and intentionally did not include an ALCI so that you would just buy another one when it quickly fails. Either way, very shady and I'm looking into product recalls.

If it makes noise, but you still use it because your budget and options are limited, please be careful and unplug it after EVERY use. Please.
justification: The product has a fire/burn hazard due to lack of ALCI and has caused a staticky/sparking sound, but no injury has been reported. The likelihood of occurrence is high because the issue seems to be inherent in the product design.

incident_description:
Product: T3 CURL ID (https://www.t3micro.com/product/curl-id-curling-iron)
Issue Overview: This curling iron has capacitive touch buttons on the handle that turn it on/off and change the heating setting. There is a safety feature to prevent heating the curling iron prior to locking the screen from these touch inputs. That safety feature is inoperable allowing the device to be turned on accidentally and immediately begin applying heat to the device.
Who was using the product: I was.
How were the products used: curling hair.
Injuries: cooked hair. Skin burns.
How: devices safety features are not correctly functioning.


Longer Description:

The T3 CURL ID does not have physical buttons to turn it on/off but instead has capacitive touch buttons that react to any touch. These buttons can turn the device on or off as well as change the heat settings. They are placed on the front face of the handle of the curling iron - where myself and other users hold the device.

The device allows you to lock the screen to disable these buttons from accepting input. According to the manual "Note: Screen must be locked to begin heat up". This is incorrect and the curling iron begins to immediately apply heat once turned on. The device does not indicate any way to lock the screen outside of the provided paper user manual.

When I used this device without locking the screen it behaved exactly as you'd expect a curling iron to behave. It heated to the temperature selected and let me start curling my hair. The device includes two modes: It's Smart and Manual modes. I used the smart mode on it's low settings. By holding the iron the device was switched to "manual" mode (because the screen does not require being locked to operate the device). The default setting for manual mode is the maximum heat setting which the iron immediately began to heat from the 260 degrees Fahrenheit I had set it to (measured via infrared thermometer afterwards) to 400 degrees Fahrenheit. In both cases according to the product manual: no heat should have been applied at all. The devices screen was never locked during my use. The temperature of this device can change by more than 100 degrees if you touch it wrong.

This change in temperature significantly damaged my hair and could have led to serious burns or fire if I had not been exceedingly careful.
justification: The user experienced injuries including cooked hair and skin burns due to the malfunctioning safety feature of the curling iron. The likelihood of occurrence is considered possible as the issue seems to be related to the device's design and user interaction.

I have it continuously plugged in, but am very careful to turn it off when I am done using it and have it sitting on a silicone pad.  

Last week I noticed that it was quite hot, even though it had been turned off for quite a few hours and the display was not on.  When I hit the on/off button, the display light came on and the temperature very quickly started to decrease, presumably to get down to the 355F default temperature.  I turned it off again (the display light turns off which indicates that it has in fact been turned off), and checked it again after a few hours.  The same situation occurred, with it still being on, despite the display being off, and presumably continuing to heat.  Same thing happened when I turned it off, with the display coming on and the temperature decreasing.  

At that point I unplugged it.  Thankfully I always have it sitting on a silicone pad, otherwise I think the wooden surface it was on would have burned or caught fire.  I contacted the company via email and their only solution was to offer to send me a free replacement.

I know I should always unplug this item, but a few things worry me about the situation.  

1.  The company was extremely quick to offer me a free replacement for a 2-year-old item.

2.  They did not request that I return the original appliance to them in order for them to diagnose what had occurred.

3.  I also just realized that there is no Underwriters Lab logo on it.
justification: The incident involved an electrical appliance overheating after being turned off, but no injury occurred. The likelihood of occurrence is unlikely as this seems to be an isolated incident with a specific product.

incident_description:
I purchased a Revlon Hot Air Brush back in September to replace the one that had shorted out. The first dryer made a popping sound and a small spark, and then started smoking at the base of the cord attached to the dryer. I didn't think much of it at the time, and I liked the dryer so I purchased a replacement on Amazon in September 2017. A few weeks ago I was drying my hair before work, and the dryer again made a really loud popping sound and sparked pretty big and it actually burned both my right wrist and singed the rug on my bathroom floor. I immediately throw the dryer into the bath tub and unplugged it. I waited for it to cool down and took some pictures so I could send it to Revlon. They responded and wanted me to send them the dryer so they could do some testing and try and figure out why it did this. It has been about a month since this happened, and I now have a scar on my arm from this dryer.

The door to my sauna is 100% tempered glass.  I was 15 minutes into my sauna (sauna set at 140 degrees F) when the glass door spontaneously and completely shattered with a loud explosion sound.  I had to open the shattered door to get out and then glass flew in all directions totally covering my bare body with glass slivers / particles (some embedded).  I sustained numerous cuts on the back of my hands, thigh, and tops of my feet.  In one of the pictures you can see blood residue on the paper towel that my wife used to clean me.  Luckily my wife was home to place towels over the projecting glass so I could get out of the sauna without serious foot injury.  I took a long shower in an attempt to remove the small glass slivers / particles from my body but still have sensations of slivers, which I hope will subside.

This information was immediately provided to the vendor of the sauna (Blue Wave Products) and later to the on-line company we purchased the sauna from (Family Pool Fun).  Both entities appear to have taken this serious incident lightly - an incident which could have ended in a catastrophic situation.  I received no feedback from the sauna vendor what quality controls / recalls have been or plan to be taken to prevent this in the future.  They assert that nothing can be done for me because the warranty has expired.  I have contested that this is beyond a mere warranty issue - it's a liability issue.

incident_description:
This morning, while styling my hair, I got a second-degree burn    when my forearm barely glanced- literally barely touched, the barrel of my clampless curling wand. I was wearing the safety glove, but it just covers to the base of the palm. My complaint and great concern is two fold. 1. The heat-resistant glove that comes with the product insufficiently protects consumers.
2. The product seems far to hot to be handled by the average consumer. While the temperature rating states that it heats to 450 degrees Fahrenheit, I question the safety of it given the extreme likelihood of a consumer accidentally burning themselves with it.
I am a grown woman. I was not goofing off or distracted in any way when I sustained the injury to my forearm today. On one prior occasion I burned my forehead and consequently my neck when I jerked from the searing pain. Those burns were terribly painful and were red and raised for quite awhile. However, after getting the terrible blistering, larger than a quarter sized  burn today,  I concluded that this product is simply unsafe.
The heat resistant glove provides a negligible heat barrier and I'm certain that one's hand would easily be burned if it came into direct contact with the heated barrel for more than 2 seconds. I've felt the burning on my fingertips several times myself while wearing. The glove length should most definitely be extended farther down the  wrist and Into the forearm inorder to provide the adequate protection needed from the 450 degree ceramic barrel! I have used heated styling products for years with no extreme burn incidents like what I have experienced with this product. It just seems extremely dangerous. I also question the accuracy and safety of the stated heating temperature. How on earth is it considered safe for the general public? I propose that this product's safety be reevaluated.
My injury is definitely very painful. I've been taking pain medication all day and can still feel the awful burning. I have looked up burn care for when and if the large blister pops. It is swollen and feels like it has fluid. I'm fairly sure it will also leave an ugly, visible scar. I have spoken to numerous women today who all share burn stories from using similar products. Some say my product might just be too hot, others say they have longer safety gloves. Taking their comments and my experience into consideration I decided to take action and report to your agency today.
justification: The incident resulted in a second-degree burn, indicating a moderate to severe injury. The likelihood of occurrence is high given the multiple burn incidents reported by the user and others with similar products.

incident_description:
I've had my Hot Tools Ionic hair dryer (model 1063) for probably five years. This morning I was drying my hair and noticed a little smoke and turned it off immediately. I looked it over and didn't notice anything so turned it back on and within 10 or 15 seconds, it caught fire at the base of the dryer, in the rubbarized area where the cord begins to come out of the handle.

I immediately yanked the plug out of the outlet. The cord was obviously very hot and it was breaking open, exposing the wires.

I'm just incredibly fortunate that I was using the dryer when it happened and it wasn't my seven-year-old daughter or the outcome could have been devastatingly different. My hair dryer is a beauty tool that I use almost daily. When I buy a new one, I don't necessarily expect it to last more than four or five years, but I definitely don't expect it to catch fire.
justification: The incident involved a hair dryer catching fire, but the user turned it off immediately and yanked the plug out of the outlet, resulting in no injury. The likelihood of occurrence is unlikely as it was a one-time event with a specific product.

incident_description:
On 2/25/2017 I was using an InStyler Auto Curler Tulip curling wand when a dangerous incident occurred as a result of using the wand.

The product was purchased by myself brand new from the store and it's seal was intact at time of purchase. Prior to using it the first time, I got out the instruction booklet that came with the wand and read it page by page, as I had never used a curling wand like it and wanted to make sure I did everything correct. To use the product, one places a strand of hair (there is a little guide included to ensure you don't put too much hair in the unit, which I was using) into the unit, pushes and holds a button. The wand automatically draws up hair into unit for a preset amount of time, at which point it beeps and you pull hair out to reveal a curl.

I had done several curls and thought I was getting the hang of it. I loaded another strand of hair into the wand, making sure I used the guide first, and the pushed the button. It pulled a little bit of hair into it then suddenly jammed, leaving it stuck on my hair with some of it sitting right on the 430 degree barrel, as I was unable to get it off. My friend who was at my home visiting helped me and we grabbed my hair with one hand and pulled the unit with the other and it let go of my hair, but not before it burned the portion touching the barrel beyond repair. I was shaken by the incident. I got back out the instruction booklet and read it once more trying to figure out where I want wrong.

There are no warnings on the box about the device having a potential to jam hair. In the user manual there is only a small warning that states "In the unlikely event of a tangle.." which made me feel a little relief thinking it was perhaps just a fluke thing.

I gathered myself and decided to give it another try about 10 minutes later. I reloaded a different section of hair into the device just as I had all the other curls, pushed the button, and it began pulling my hair into the wand. Then all of a sudden, again, my hair jammed with so much force that it hurt my scalp. I tried to pull the wand off my hair like the last time, but it was to no avail. The hair would not come out of the wand. I was freaking out. A large portion of my hair was wrapped around the hot barrel. My friend rushed over again to try and help me pull it off my hair but it was not budging. The more I pulled at the hot wand, the more it pulled at my scalp and the more pain it caused. I began crying and frantically trying to get it off my hair as I smelled it begin to burn it. I yanked the cord out of the wall. My friend grabbed a pair of scissors nearby and and to cut my hair. We had no other choice. This left me with a section of hair now cut half way up that looks absolutely ridiculous and also left me feeling pain on my scalp where we had pulled to try and get it off for a couple hours after the incident.
justification: The incident resulted in injury, as the user experienced hair loss, scalp pain, and emotional distress. The likelihood of occurrence is unlikely, as the user followed instructions and had not heard of similar incidents.

incident_description:
On the evening of January 19th, 2016, I purchased a Revlon hair dryer from the Target in Medina, MN. After I returned home that night, I tried to use this hair dryer to blow dry my daughter's hair after she showered. I plugged it in and turned in on and immediately the hair dryer shot out fire.
My coat sleeve and my arm were both set on fire. I ran my arm under water. My daughter screamed and started crying. I was in great pain and was irritated by the Target. So I went to the Target to talk to the manager and explain the issue to him. At that time I noticed that the hair dryer seemed to have been used for a very long time. The handle was badly worn, the paint was off or faded, and it was repackaged. The Target manager was not sympathetic and was not willing to help me. He suggested me to contact the manufacturer of the dryer.

The pain kept getting worse at night, and I went to the urgent care the next day. The doctor gave me medications and a shot and I returned home. The next few days my arm became infected and the pain was getting even worse. I went to the urgent care again and the doctor diagnosed it as Second Degree Burn and Wound Infection, for which I was given more medications. In the
next three weeks, the infection and pain prevented me from doing most of my routine duties during the day and from sleeping well during the night. This incident also caused an emotional stress on the whole family. My daughter sustained a fear of hair dryers for a period of time after this, afraid of using hair dryers to dry her hair.

I contacted Target headquarters about this incident, and they also directed me to the manufacturer Helen of Troy. I contacted the manufacturer who asked me to mail in the hair dryer. However, I think it is the main evidence of this incident so I have been hesitant to mail it in. I have sought help from two different lawyers but neither was able to help. I believe that this incident should not have happened had either Target or the manufacturer been responsible. And I believe that by making both parties more responsible, it will help protect the rights of all the consumers and
customers of the two parties.
justification: The incident resulted in a second-degree burn and wound infection, causing injury to the individual. The likelihood of such an incident occurring is unlikely, as it involved a specific product malfunction.

incident_description:
I had been blow drying my hair in my bedroom for about 8 minutes when I suddenly saw, out of the corner of my eye, an orange flash of light coming from the hair dryer. I simultaneously heard a sizzling, crackling sound coming from the dryer. It scared me, and I immediately turned it off and unplugged it.

-	I did not feel my hair being pulled, and I did not smell anything burning, so IÃÂm sure there was no hair caught in the dryer. (IÃÂve had a piece of hair get caught in a dryer before during my lifetime, and I could feel it pull my hair out, and I could smell burning hair for a moment. That has not happened in a long time, and I donÃÂt remember if it has ever happened with this dryer or not.)
-	I usually blow dry my hair for about 10 minutes almost every night. My hair is long, and thick, and completely natural. I use no leave-in products on my hair.
-	I do not remember how long I have had this dryer, but I will estimate about 4 years, maybe.
-	I checked the lint filter on the dryer, and it was not significantly blocked, as you can see from one of the attached images.
-	The ALCI plug did not trip, nor did the [REDACTED] Grounded power strip that I had the dryer plugged into.
-	I later noticed that the power cord coming out of the 2 inch rubber cord protector (I donÃÂt know what itÃÂs called) at the base of the dryer had partially melted, and you can just barely see a piece of copper wire showing through, and that the cord at that point appears to be permanently twisted about 90 degrees clockwise. (See attached images.)
-	Up until last year I did not realize dryer cords were not supposed to be wrapped around the dryer. So it is possible that years of wrapping a warm cord around the dryer for storage caused the cord to become twisted and weakened at that particular spot that melted. That may potentially have contributed to the dryer sparking.

However, despite my ignorance, I still feel this is a potential health hazard for consumers due to the significant number of similar and worse incidents reported on this sight and online from use of hair dryers of several different manufacturers.

Accolades to hair dryer manufacturers and government regulators for ALCI plugs, cord protectors, cleanable filters, safety warning labels, and safety instructions. Chi does state in their safety instructions #5: ÃÂKeep the cord away from heated surfaces. Do not wrap the cord around the appliance.ÃÂ (See attached images.)

However, I donÃÂt know any consumer that wants their hair dryer to be hanging up on their wall as a permanent part of their bedroom or bathroom decor. That would be a potential hazard also, because of all the constant dust getting into the vents. Most non-professional consumers store their blow dryers in a cabinet or drawer, and that requires folding up the cords to some extent, causing some twisting, even if they are careful to not twist the cord tightly around the appliance. I think this is conceivably and reasonably evident due to the significant number of similar and worse incidents reported online.

To protect the interests of all hair dryer manufacturers, and to prevent serious injuries to consumers in the future due to this issue, I would recommend that the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission require hair dryer manufacturers to manufacture stronger hair dryer power cords, or require that they include with the dryer some sort of simple storage tray or wall mount that would prevent cord folding or twisting.
justification: The incident involved a hair dryer sparking and making a sizzling sound, but the user immediately turned it off and unplugged it without injury. The likelihood of occurrence is considered possible due to the user's frequent use of the dryer and similar incidents reported online.

incident_description: On April 21, 2015 at approximately 8:15 p.m., I purchased a Revlon hairdryer from Walgreens store #[REDACTED] at 1300 Hazelwood Drive in Smyrna, Tennessee, model number RV474 for $19.99 plus tax.  A copy of the receipt is attached hereto as Exhibit 1.  A photograph of the hairdryer in its original packaging is attached hereto as Exhibit 2.   I left the hair dryer in its original packaging until the next morning, the morning of April 22, 2015.   At approximately 7:20 a.m., when I was ready to dry my hair, I unpacked the hair dryer, removed the plastic piece covering the prongs of the plug, plugged it in and turned on the hairdryer.  Immediately flames shot out of the front of the hairdryer where the air comes out.  Four separate burning particles flew out of the hairdryer and landed in three separate locations: one inside a basket near my vanity, two on the edge of a wooden vanity seat, and one on the bathroom floor.   The particles were not simply smoldering, but were actually actively burning with flames present.  I extinguished the particles that I could find immediately, (the one on the floor and the two on the vanity seat) and discovered that each burning particle was a tiny metal ring that had obviously shot out of the dryer.  I was aware of a burning smell, and upon further investigation found the fourth particle that had burned a hole through the side of the basket near my vanity.   I immediately unplugged the hairdryer for fear of injury, and was afraid to use it.   After attempting to clean the burned areas, repackaging the hairdryer, taking photographs of the damage, and locating my receipt, I plugged my electric toothbrush into the same socket of the same plug, and there were no issues, confirming to me that there was no problem with my outlet, and that the flames were a result of a faulty and dangerous hairdryer.  Moreover, I recently had an electrical inspection by a certified and licensed electrician, in which no problems with the outlet in which the hairdryer was plugged were discovered, further underscoring the certainty that the damage was the result of a faulty, defective, and dangerous product.

Upon examination, it appears the wiring is down to bare wires in one location on the electrical cord.  This hair dryer is a "cord keeper" hair dryer whereby the cord retracts into the unit.
justification: The hair dryer produced sparks and had exposed wiring, posing a hazard, but there was no injury. The likelihood of occurrence is considered possible due to the existing damage to the cord.

incident_description:
Not long ago, my Revlon hairdryer started having some issues (the plug in had to be wiggled a lot for their to be a full connection to the outlet and maintain power).  So, I opted to replace it.  I chose another Revlon product, having been generally satisfied with my previous model (I actually bought that one twice).  Anyway, the replacement was a Revlon Ionic 1875W model, that came in a turquoise color.  

Recently, I started using the medium setting vs. the high setting, so that I can hear my radio when getting ready in the morning.  Over the last few days of use , I noticed that the "high" setting, was actually feeling more like "medium".  The button was set to high flow, but was not coming out as such.

The hair dryer also started intermittently changing heat settings, it would be warm, then hot, or give me a shot of cold, or whatever it felt like doing.  No discernible pattern, that I could tell.  The issue only happened a few times, and I couldn't make it repeat on purpose.  But, I did start paying attention to it, because it was just weird.

Today, everything changed.  I typically dry my hair most of the way without styling tools, and just when it's almost done I use a round brush to style it.  I started with the front bang area of my hair, everything seemed fine.  Two round brushes further back, I noticed a smell.  Burnt smell.  I turned the hairdryer off and set it down.  Started brushing my hair and saw a big glob of hair on my brush.  Pulled it out and put it in the sink.  Started running my fingers through my hair, and pulled out chunks (that somewhat resemble a hair extension with glue on the root end).  Chunks were coming out, strands were coming out, and tiny pieces were breaking off as I touched the root ends of my hair.  It was very alarming.

I have very fine, very thin hair.  I'm in my mid 40's, so I'm well aware of how to blow dry & style my hair.  I know not to stay in one spot for long, and I didn't do that in this case either.  I wear my hair just past my shoulders (appx 2.5-inches), in a slightly layered style.

I have a small spot just above the bang line where the hair was burnt down near the scalp.  That area is maybe an eighth of an inch long.  Another area, which is quite a bit larger, is at the top/crown of my head.  Most of that hair is burned down to less than half of an inch long.  There may be a few strands longer (hard for me to see).  But, the area itself is approximately the size of golf ball.   The third and largest area, is damaged and still falling out.  The best way to describe location on this, is half way between the crown & nape of my neck.  In this area, the hair is damaged, and like I said, still falling out.  The most disturbing part about this last area described, is that I hadn't started styling that area yet.  So, either a spark flew down from when I was styling the top, or it flew up when I was doing a general dry and moving all around.  Either way, it's scary to thing that this incident could actually have been worse.

I have emailed Revlon, and am awaiting their specific response (only had an auto email so far).  

This unit isn't that old - a few months or so?  I'd have to try to locate my receipt, and I'm not sure that I have it.  It's not a heavy use item either.  One person usage, approximately 5 days a week for 5-10 minutes off & on.  I don't dry & style at the exact same time.  And, I rarely use on the weekends.  So, in my opinion, this is a potentially serious & dangerous equipment malfunction - not user error.

I would like to recommend investigation and recall of this unit.
justification: The hairdryer malfunctioned, causing burns to the user's hair and scalp, resulting in hair loss and damage. The incident appears to be an isolated event, with no indication of frequent or widespread issues.

incident_description:
Revlon Hair Dryer Model RVDR5141 has a risk of electrocution.

We started using this hair dryer about one month ago.  As we used it, the motor started cutting out more and more frequently.  I thought that there must be a loose connection inside, until I saw smoke and sparks where the electrical cord entered the rubber stress relief tube on the handle.  The electrical  cord was about to break in two.  Bare copper wire was exposed from both leads.

I started to re-package the hair dryer in its original box and noticed that the box will not close unless the power cord is bent at a sharp 90 angle where the cord enters the stress relief tube.  I have surmised that there are two problems.  1.)  The extension cord insulation is made of a more brittle and less flexible material than other cords, and 2.)  The box the hair dryer is packaged in is too small and forces the power cord to be bent severely, in order to close the box.  This severe bend essentially breaks the cord insulation.

Please take action to force this company to issue a RECALL.  Many other consumers are experiencing the same problem and nothing is being done about it.  Revlon is clearly not taking any responsibility based upon their corporate BS response.
justification: The incident involved a hair dryer with exposed copper wire and visible smoke and sparks, posing an electrocution risk, but no injury was reported. The likelihood of occurrence is high due to multiple consumers experiencing the same problem.

incident_description: I received a CHI hair dryer for Christmas, purchased from Sam's Club.  When I use it, my hair is almost dry and it takes me less than 5 minutes to use a round brush and finish styling my hair by drying it with the dryer.  For storage, the dryer has been hung on my wall by the loop the manufacturer provides that is permanently attached to the dryer.  The cord is not wrapped or anything.  Today I was drying my hair and had been using the dryer probably 3 minutes when I noticed an orange spark fly out of the dryer.  I held it away from my hair, in front of my view, and tried to turn it off.  I accidentally turned it to low instead of off (the switch position is low to one side, high to the other, off in the center).  Another spark flew out before I could get the dryer turned off and unplugged.  I was very startled.  I believe this could easily have set my hair on fire and have never had a hair dryer do this before.  Since the dryer was only 8 months old and in perfect condition, I believe this is a serious safety issue and a recall should probably be issued.  I will be returning the item to Sam's Club as soon as possible.

incident_description:

This was the first time the consumer used a BIC Soleil razor in over 2 years. The consumer use to use them and would always get open wounds on both her legs but during these past 2 years the consumer has not had an open wound. The consumer states she suffered from these open wounds for about 18 months while using BIC Soleil razors. The consumer visited many dermatologists to find what caused her to get the open wounds on her legs but she was never told a reason. With this recent incident the consumer has realized that the BIC Soleil razors are the cause for the open wounds on her legs. The consumer states the wounds vary in size and could be as small as a dime and as big as a quarter. The consumer states pus comes out of the wound and a little bit of blood.

The consumer believes these razors should be investigated because they pose a safety hazard. The consumer plans to have the razor tested.

The consumer only has the razor she used on 05/27/15 and no longer has the package where the razor came in. The consumer believes the razor was purchased approximately 4 years ago. 

On 06/03/15 the consumer sent an email to the firm to inform them of her safety concerns. The consumer has not received a response as of today, 06/04/15.

Additions to report.  These sores are extremely painful/sensitive to touch.  Approx 1 tsp toseveral tablespoons of pus is exuded.  It takes 4-6wks to resolve and heal leaving scar.  The consumer currently has 1 remaining open sore from the incident on 5/27/15.
justification: The consumer suffered open wounds, pus, and bleeding after using the razor, indicating an injury. The consumer has experienced similar incidents in the past with the same product, suggesting a recurring issue.

incident_description:
Revlon RV544PKF 1875W Tourmaline Ionic Ceramic Dryer

I purchased this unit in November 2014 from Amazon.  Only lasted 6 months.  I turned it on the other day and it didn't work.  I thought the GFCI was tripped so I pressed the button...that was not the issue.  I then tried the power switch again and a huge spark and smoke came from the area where the cord enters the dryer. incident_description:
On January 12, 2013, my 8-year old son went skiing with our neighbors.  Our neighbor had put Little Hotties Toe Warmers on my son's socks.  While my son was putting his foot into his ski boot, the toe warmer came unattached from the sock and ended up between my son's shin and the front of the ski boot.  Within an hour, my son asked one of the ski instructors to help him with his boot, and they took the toe warmer out.  Although my son was wearing socks and the toe warmer did not come in contact with his skin, he ended up with a 2nd and 3rd degree burn and was unable to participate in skiing for the remainder of the season, as well as other physical activities, like swimming.  Attached is a picture I took just more than 2 weeks after the incident occurred.  We took my son to his pediatrician, however after 3 visits were referred to 2 different emergency rooms and then to the Burn Clinic, where he was treated by burn specialist over the course of approximately 4 months.

Although there are some warnings posted on the outside of the Little Hotties Toe Warmer packages, I never would have anticipated this type of injury.  Needless to say, this was my son's first experience with toe warmers and will be his last.
justification: The incident resulted in a 2nd and 3rd degree burn, which required medical treatment and impacted the child's activities for several months, but did not result in death. The incident was an unexpected event given the product's intended use and warnings.

incident_description: The incident involves a Revlon RV484 Hair Dryer. The hair Dryer was bought new approx one year ago and has been used daily since it was purchased. On the incident date, when my wife was using the hair dryer, it began to vary in speed and power by itself, then began cycling off and on during use, until the unit failed completely. I took a look at the hair dryer and could see that the wire insulation looked like it was failing where it enters the strain relief on the hair dryer handle. I took apart the hair dryer and tested the components with a multimeter. I isolated the failure as an intermittent break in the copper wiring under the insulation. By twisting the cord while connected to the meter, I could make or break continuity. The insulation, which appears to be a rubber-like material, at the point of failure appeared deteriorated. The remainder of the wire insulation (the complete six feet from the integrated GFCI to where the cord enters the hair dryer) just didn't look right either. It wasn't as deteriorated as the insulation at the point of the wire failure, but it appears to look like the early stages of deterioration. Thinking that this hair dryer power cord failure was just a fluke, I went onto amazon.com to read reviews about this particular hair dryer to see if others had experienced this failure. I found that mine was NOT an isolated incident. Others have had the same issue with the power cord, including smoking and sparking, from the wire insulation failing where the cord enter the handle of the hair dryer.
justification: The incident involved a product failure with no reported injury, but potential for harm exists due to insulation failure and user exposure to electrical components. The likelihood of occurrence is considered likely due to multiple reports of similar issues with the same product model.

On March 1, 20141 used my Conair hair dryer, model number 070RW, after showering. When finished drying my hair, I switched the dryer off and proceeded to finish shaving and brushing my teeth. About ten minutes elapsed since I had switched off the hair dryer when I heard a whooshing sound. At first I was uncertain where the sound was coming  from but quickly saw that it was the hair dryer. The dryer had self started. Smoke and a bluish flame was rising from the handle area of the dryer. I immediately pulled the dryer plug from the wall outlet.

The smoke and flame subsided. At no time was the dryer exposed to any water or moisture. The dryer spontaneously self started with the switch in the off position. I was thankful that I was still in the bathroom when the incident occurred and could disconnect the dryer before it could start the house on fire. The outlet where the dryer was connected is on a GFI circuit.

On March 3, 2014, I reported this incident by phone to [REDACTED], Conair Claims Manager at her office in Stamford
Connecticut [REDACTED]. [REDACTED] said she would send me a shipping carton to send the unit back to them for analysis. So far, I have not received anything.

The consumer immediately unplugged the hair dryer from the wall outlet.  The consumer said that approximately 50% of the cord is burned in that area and it is now held on by a string.

incident_description:
I received a package of Scunci no-slip grip hair bands in December.  I slept with one in back in March and as result, I have lost a patch of hair.  On the morning after I slept with it in, my head was sore and indented.  A few days later, the area was red and swollen.  A few weeks later, I noticed my hair was falling out then noticed a distinct (about 2 inch) line in my head where I was missing hair.  I went to a Dr. for this and she believes the hair loss is due to sleeping with the hair band.  She couldn't tell me if it was due to contact dermatitis, as the hair band has an open area on the back that is the no-slip grip or due to the compression and the band being too tight.  I received steroid injections in my head with the hope that it will restore the hair, but the dermatologist couldn't give me a definitive that it will grow back.
I have email the company two times requesting material information, but have yet to receive a response.
justification: The incident resulted in hair loss and scalp irritation, which constitutes an injury. The likelihood of occurrence is considered unlikely as it was a single incident reported by the individual.

incident_description:
I purchased a WAHL Groom Pro Head & Total Body Grooming Kit (it includes a hair clipper, trimmer, multiple attachments, and a carrying case) at Walmart located at 1220 Old Country Rd, Westbury, NY 11590.  I also purchased from the same store the WAHL Total Care cleaning spray which is designed to clean the hair clipper.  I purchased both products approximately one year ago.  

In the early morning hours of April 5, 2013, at approximately 1:40 AM, I was sitting in my bedroom in my house cleaning the WAHL hair clipper.  I had just used it minutes before to trim my chest hair.  I was cleaning the hair clipper using the WAHL ÃÂTotal CareÃÂ all in one cleaner, lubricant, & coolant spray.  I purchased the WAHL cleaning spray because I had assumed that the spray made by WAHL would be the best product to use to clean the WAHL hair clipper.  

I followed the instructions on the spray can exactly.  The WAHL Total Care spray can states, ÃÂTurn unit off and brush hair from blades.  Next, holding the unit in a downward position and with the unit running, liberally apply solution to blades to completely flush out all foreign matter.  Allow Wahl Total care to remain on the blades for 2 minutes.  Turn unit off and wipe clean.  Unit is ready for use.ÃÂ  I brushed hair from the blades while it was off.  I turned the clipper on, held it in a downward position while still running, and I began to liberally apply the solution to the blades.  At that exact moment, the head and blades of the hair clipper caught on fire.  

I attempted to blow out the fire, and it would not blow out.  I had been cleaning the hair clipper over my garbage can.  After I realized I could not blow the fire out, I dropped the flaming hair clipper into my garbage can to avoid being burned while in a state of panic.  I had no safer place available to drop the flaming hair clipper.  The only alternative place to drop it would have been my bedroom floor, and this might have caused my entire house to catch fire.  After dropping the flaming hair clipper into my garbage, the contents of my garbage caught on fire, and in a moment a very large fire was inside my garbage bin.  My garbage bin is a large approximately 13 gallon plastic garbage bin I previously purchased from Target.  I began to shout ÃÂFireÃÂ and my mother and brother came running to my room with fire extinguishers.  They used the fire extinguishers to put out the fire in my garbage.  The garbage was still smoking after the fire was extinguished, so I then poured water inside the garbage.  Fortunately, the fire went out.  I placed the smokey garbage bin and clipper outside my house, because I was afraid it would reignite.    

As a result of the fire, my entire bedroom, and the second and third floors of my house were filled with smoke.  We opened all the windows and waited for the smoke to dissipate while choking on smoke in the air.  When the smoke finally dissipated, I saw that my entire room was covered in a layer of smoke dust/residue.  I have numerous electronics in my bedroom (television, desktop computer, laptop, printer, speakers, cable box, DVR, blu-ray player) and I do not yet know what effect this residue will have on my electronics.  Furthermore, I believe it is likely my room will need to be professionally cleaned.  I also do not know whether I will need medical treatment, as I unavoidably and inadvertently breathed in a large amount of smoke during the fire.  I do not yet know the full extent of the damage of this fire.
justification: The incident involved a fire that caused property damage and smoke inhalation, but no injury was reported. The use of fire extinguishers and ventilation prevented further harm.

incident_description:
Saturday morning, 1/26/2013, I was drying my hair about 7:15 a.m. using my approx. 6-month old Helen of Troy tangle-free thermal hot air brush. It takes about 20 minutes to dry my hair, and I usually read the paper or a book while running the brush through my hair. I just turn my hair under so it's pretty easy to use. My hair was almost dry when I noticed white globs caught in the curls. I was trying to figure out what they were when I looked down at the hair dryer and noticed that there was a large hole melted into the plastic brush. I immediately turned off and unplugged the dryer; the brush and tip were burning hot to my touch. I think in another second or so my hair might have caught fire. I worked to free what I realized were parts of the brush that had melted in my hair. I do feel very lucky not to have been injured, though I tore some hair pulling out the plastic bits. I was going to a meeting so I plugged in a different brush dryer and finished my hair.

I've taken pictures of the flecks in my hair that remained last night after removing most everything else. I also took pictures of the hair dryer.

I think the dryer overheated but the reset button did not shut it down. 

I've used dryers like this for many years, and during this time have gone through seven or eight of the lower-cost [REDACTED] models. These do overheat and will shut down until they've cooled down. If they do that several times, it's my cue to toss the dryer and replace it with another from my stock (several years ago I bought about ten [REDACTED] dryers on sale at WalMart, but I haven't found them there in years). 

However, the Helen of Troy is a Professional model and had never shut off/overheated during the six months or so I've owned it. I liked it very much. In the last week, however, I had noticed that the plastic had become discolored, and I had planned to take off the roller brush this weekend to clean it. The only hair product I use is [REDACTED] shampoo (I don't even use hair spray) so there was nothing new in my routine that might have caused the discoloration.

Since this is a relatively new -- just six months old -- dryer, I am wondering whether what happened to me might happen to some other user if this is a design and/or production flaw.
justification: The incident involved a hair dryer overheating and melting parts of its brush, but no injury occurred. The likelihood of this specific event is unlikely as it seems to be an isolated incident with a relatively new product.

She started gasping for air, so my husband passed the brand new aspirator to me and I went to relieve my choking panicking baby. As I squeezed the product as you normally do with an aspirator to my shock and dismay the end came clean off!

Thankfully both my husband and I are infant first aid qualified and where able to help our baby until we could relieve her breathing with the other aspirator we had been given by the hospital!
I am horrified by this product and am thankful that we knew what to do and had another aspirator to use. 
This product should not be on shelves and I have reviewed this product in numerous places warning other parents of the hazard.
Please do something about this terrible and dangerous product.

At the same time I received a terrible shock and burn to my right arm. Thank goodness my curling iron was plugged into an G.F.I. outlet, as it immediately cut the power to the curling iron and tripped the circuit breaker. I dropped the curling iron and looked at my arm and realized that I had been burned by this. I had received a shock and was obviously shook by this incident. I inspected the curling iron and where the cord meets the swivel end (to keep the cord from getting tangled), I saw that the cord had been literally blown out of the swivel and a couple of the copper wires were melted. 

I had not had any problems with this curling iron prior to this happening. No frays, no over heating, absolutely no problems prior to this. 

I did see my physician for the burn who told me that it was definitely an electrical burn and that I needed to watch it carefully for 24-48 hours to make sure that the tissue under my skin is not damaged. 

I did some research online on this model and there are numerous reports of the same thing happening to others as well.

While doing some research online she noticed that other consumers experienced the same failure with the same model dryer. She indicate d that after reading the reports and the firm did not offer any of the consumers any assistance that she was not going to contact them.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning blow dryer that started to melt, posing a fire hazard, but did not result in any injury. The fact that other consumers experienced the same failure with the same model dryer suggests that the issue may not be isolated.

incident_description:
We bought an Infiniti hair straightening iron for our daughter, but it has stopped regulating temperature and only goes to the hottest setting.

This is a real safety hazard.  If the product fails, it should stop heating, not go to full heat.
justification: The incident describes a product malfunction that could potentially cause harm, but no injury has occurred yet. The likelihood of occurrence is considered possible as the product is still in use and may cause harm if not properly addressed.

incident_description:
While drying her hair, my wife noticed a burning smell. When she pulled the dryer away from her head to examine it and with the dryer fan still operating, flames began to shoot 2 to 3 inches out of the nozzle. She had to pull the plug to disconnect the device. Had she not noticed the smell, she most likely would have been burned. There was no apparent breaker switch that activated.

The product was purchased approximately 2 years ago as is a dryer sold by Jerdon Products of Richardson, Texas and was marketed under the name "First Class". It's model number is JWM6CF
justification: The incident involved a hair dryer emitting flames, but no injury occurred because the user promptly reacted. The likelihood of occurrence is considered possible given the malfunction of a consumer product.

incident_description:
Product was used by myself in accordance with all safety instructions. Was used on the genitals for several minutes, as the product was designed to be used. Personal lubrication was used which on previous usage by itself did not cause any problems. Product was used one time for 5 to 10 minutes with direct skin contact and rubbing on the penis, and then subsequently discarded. Immediately experienced cough, difficulty breathing, sick feeling in stomach, and headache. Symptoms continued for several days and worsened into sore throat, severe coughing, loose stools, and irritation of the penis, excessive urination, spontaneous constriction of genitals. Genitals coated with an oily chemical residue that is highly resistant to removal from the skin. This acute phase lasted for several weeks, and less severe symptoms persist after several months.

This is the third time I have used this product (in three years, each time purchasing a new one) and had nearly identical symptoms each time. Manufacturer insists it could not have been caused by their product. Urinalysis on two separate occasions showed no bacterial infection, but traces of blood in urine. Chemical composition of product is manufacturer secret, and they claim it's not made from latex or silicone, and that it's non-allergenic and phthalate-free. Allergist cannot confirm allergy due to unknown ingredients.

The majority of users of this product have not reported any similar problems. I believe in certain conditions this product is highly dangerous to human health, whether a person has an allergy, a person is genetically predisposed to having a sensitivity to the product, accidental misuse, errors in manufacturing, contaminated source materials used in manufacturing, or other unknown factors.
justification: The user experienced severe symptoms including cough, difficulty breathing, and genital irritation after using the product, indicating a significant injury. The likelihood of occurrence is unlikely as the majority of users have not reported similar problems.

incident_description:
Vidal Sassoon 1875 IONIC Hairdryer 

Inside of dryer caught fire burning my hair. Black smoke was pouring out of dryer. Unsafe product!
justification: The incident resulted in an injury, as the fire burned the user's hair. The likelihood of this occurrence is unlikely, as it is a singular reported incident with the product.

incident_description: Hair dryer caught fire while unattended.  Self extinguished.  Left cloud of noxious smoke which took 2 days to air out; most of the smell is gone now but still is in clothes.
justification: The incident involved a fire and noxious smoke but did not result in injury, hence severity level 2. The likelihood is unlikely as the incident occurred under specific conditions (unattended hair dryer) and self-extinguished.

incident_description:
I was using the AirCut as advertised. I wet my hair in the sink. Rubbed lubricating oil on the blades prior to use and then washed my hands. While using the product, the AC adapter fell in the wet sink. I quickly unplugged the product from the wall. The adapter began sending out sparks from the sink. 

This is a horribly designed product. I looked at similar products and neither of them have an AC adapter. I also looked at hair dryers, which are also similar in shape and size. I am not sure why the company advertises that you can use the product anywhere, especially when a mirror is needed and they recommend you wash your hair.
justification: The incident involved an electrical shock hazard with sparks, but no injury was reported. The likelihood of such an incident occurring is unlikely given proper use and precautions.

incident_description: The Philips Norelco Rechargeable Tripleheader Cordless Razor which I just purchased, exploded in my hands as I was shaving.  This was a mechanical spring-loaded type event which sent the razor edged shaving wheels into my face and around the room.  I have photos.  This product could easily blind someone!
justification: The incident involved a physical injury from the razor's shaving wheels, but the severity is not life-threatening. The likelihood of this specific mechanical failure occurring is unlikely, as it is not a commonly reported issue with this product.

incident_description:
I bought my wife a Conair ION Hot Hair Rollers. This product is less than one year old.
One morning about a week ago I heard something making a popping noise.
We were not sure what it was. Than I smelled something and went toward the bathroom to investigate.

Thats when I discovered the Conair Hair Rollers were on fire and blazing.
I unplugged and tried to put out the fire. As the rollers were still blazing I picked up the conair and ran out the back door to keep from catching the bathroom on fire.

I reported this to Conair by email over a week ago and am amazed that no one has called or emailed me back concerning this matter.
justification: The incident involved a product malfunction leading to a fire, but no injury was reported. The likelihood of such an event happening again is unlikely given that it's a singular reported incident.

incident_description:
Consumer stated that while he was using the power razor to shave one of the blades disintegrated (top blade) which caused him to receive lacerations to the right side of his face.

Consumer visited his physician to examine the wound, it didnot need any stitches or medical treatment.

10/26/11 Consumer contacted the manufacturer and was advised that he should keep the product so that their safety team could examine it.

Consumer is concerned that this razor is a safety hazard and should be reported
justification: The consumer received lacerations to the right side of his face, which is an injury, thus severity level 3. The incident was a one-time event and not described as part of a larger pattern, making the likelihood of occurrence unlikely, or level 2.

incident_description:
My hot tools curling iron model 1141 emitted a bright red flash and a loud explosive sound which made my ears ring.  It had been preheated for under 10 minutes at the mid-point setting.  Fortunately it was in my hand and not near my head. It is UL listed 575T; type PB1141WS E65995.

I am not a "local government agency" though your form automatically indicated that I am.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning curling iron that emitted a loud noise and a bright flash, but fortunately, it was being held and not near the user's head, and no injury was reported. The user's hearing was temporarily affected but no lasting injury resulted.

incident_description: I have a ÃÂ3m tekk protectionÃÂ ear muffs for sound protection while leaf blowing. It has a ÃÂansi s3.19 1994ÃÂ on it. As I was putting them on the plastic strap across the top that holds them together snapped. When it did the broken ends it struck me on the head. Fortunately it did not cut me. If I had hair to push back, as a woman might have, they may have pulled them apart in front of their face possibly damaging an eye. The product has only been used 6 times at the most.
justification: The incident involved a product failure that could have potentially caused injury, but did not result in any actual harm. The likelihood of such an occurrence is unlikely given the product has only been used 6 times.

incident_description: The consumer stated that her curling iron poses a potential burn hazard because the clamp of the curling iron is far too short. The consumer stated that the clamp, that would trap hair in between the clamp and the iron is so short that the consumer has to place the iron very close to their skin. justification: The consumer suffered a burn on her right arm, but it was not serious and did not require medical attention. The likelihood of this occurrence is unlikely as there is no indication of a widespread issue with the product.

incident_description: When using my Revlon hairdryer today, sizeable sparks/fire were emitted from the dryer.  My natural reflex was to drop the dryer, thereby burning my carpeting.  I did not suffer an injury. I have reported this incident to Revlon and am awaiting a response.
justification: The incident involved sparks/fire and property damage, but no injury occurred. The likelihood of such an event is unlikely given that hairdryers are common and such incidents are not typical.

incident_description: Conair Hair Dryer model 228GDC was sitting on top of a counter . It was there for at least 2 days (we were out of town) when we returned there was a burn mark that was caused by an electrical problem where the power cord enters the dryer (there is a rotating ball at this position) The plastic in this area is burned and melted. If this had been sitting on a towel or other flammable material it could have caused a fire. I still have the hair dryer.
justification: The incident involved a hair dryer with a burned and melted power cord area, but there was no injury reported. The likelihood of occurrence is rare as it was a one-time event with no indication of repeated issues.

incident_description: While using the dryer there was a loud pop and electronic "fireball" that came from the handle.  The unit then, of course, quit working and the handle is slightly scorched right where it folds.  The switch will not physically move now.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning dryer with a loud pop and electronic 'fireball', but there was no reported injury. The damage was limited to the dryer unit and its handle.

incident_description: I was using the Vidal Sassoon 1875 Ionic hair dryer when a large spark flew over the top of my head.
justification: The incident involved a spark, indicating a potential hazard, but there is no mention of injury. The likelihood of such an event is unlikely as it is not a common occurrence with normal use of a hair dryer.

incident_description: While drying hair on high setting, the handle of the dryer becomes extremely hot and cannot be held in hand.
justification: The incident involves a hair dryer with an extremely hot handle, but no injury is reported. The likelihood of this occurrence is considered possible as it can happen when using the dryer on a high setting.

incident_description:
I was injured while showering, with a bar of Ivory Soap by a foreign, near razor sharp fragment of metal, protruding
from within a newly opened bar. I was washing my body with the soap bar in my hand when I noticed blood and felt stinging pain. The metal fragment was stIckIng out of the soap after the bar started to melt away as a result of my rubbing the bar on my skin to wash. The metal fragment appears to be molded into the entire mIddle of the bar.
Before I was actually aware of what was happening, I had several scratches and some rather deep lacerations on
a large portion of my chest, arms and legs requiring medIcal attention.
justification: The incident resulted in injury with several scratches and deep lacerations requiring medical attention. The presence of a metal fragment in a soap bar is unexpected and unusual.

incident_description:
While blow drying my hair, the Revlon Model RV484 - 1875 W 125 Vac 60 Hz - Helen of Troy - Made in China model blew up in my face with sparks showering into my face and neck.  The failure site was where the cord fed up into the unit.  I was not in the practice of coiling this cord up. I did notice there was no strain relief at this site..The unit had only been in use for six months. This is a potentially very dangerous situation. I was fortunate because I had a GFI on the electrical outlet to power the unit.

More Model information....Intertek 3175842 - Type Rd484FA
justification: The incident involved a blow dryer blowing up with sparks, but the person was not injured, likely due to the presence of a GFI on the electrical outlet. The failure occurred at the cord feed site, which lacked strain relief.

incident_description: When using my hair dryer Conair Ionshine 1875, model # 146ZDFR the cord as it enters the heavier rubber part of the cord at the dryer end erupted in sparks and seperated partially from the drier/cord on one strand of the wire. Upon returning from a weekend trip to Massachusetts I found out my daughter had the very same thing happen to her with the very same dryer. I have contacted the company to no avail. This is a serious flaw in that design and could be fatal if not handled properly. I have the dryer and intedn to keep until the company has contacted me about it.
justification: The incident involved a hair dryer cord erupting in sparks and partially separating from the dryer, but no injury was reported. The potential for injury or death was noted, but it did not occur.

incident_description: Dryer is too hot to hold within a few minutes of being on hot and high setting.  Seam on the dryer handle has also seperated due to the intensity of the heat.
justification: The dryer being too hot to hold and having a separated handle seam indicates an incident with potential for injury, but no injury reported. The conditions suggest a possible risk of injury if used extensively.

incident_description:
Remington Pearl Ceramic Ultimate T Studio 20 hair rollers.
1. The ends of each roller will burn fingertips. They did mine. One would think that companies that make hair rollers would want to use a heat resistant plastic to make the ends out of, since they know their customers are in contact with the ends of the rollers than any other part of the roller. 

2. These rollers sit on metal rods that heat up each roller. The last time I used the product I was unaware that some of the rollers had come off their places in the rods. I plugged unit in and went went few feet away back into the bedroom to do a few things while I waited for them to heat up.
  When I came back into bathroom I instantly smelled melting/burning plastic, lifted up the lid and found the rollers that weren't sitting on the rods like they should have been and the ends were in direct contact with the hot metal rods, and therefore melting as they were sitting against the rods.
  I unplugged it, carefully got the rollers back on the rods where they were supposed to be and swore to take it back after setting it down on my empty tub ledge to cool off. 
  I had planned on taking it back to Target where I bought it but then I got worried that even if I told the return clerk about what happened and made sure to tell them that they do not need to put them back on the shelf since they are a safety/fire risk and the ends are damaged now and the metal rods have melted plastic in some places; that the clerk would forget to pass that on to the next employee that handled it and it would be put back on the shelf.
justification: The incident involved damage to the product and a potential safety risk, but no injury occurred. The likelihood of occurrence is considered possible due to the described malfunction and user error.

incident_description:
A very large electrical spark (looked like an orange fireball) exploded out of my Revlon curling iron model RV051 while I was styling my hair. Luckily the spark went away from my face and I was not burned. However, I have searched online and found others have had similar problems with Revlon curling irons.

I contacted Revlon regarding the problem and they passed me along to the company they said makes these curling irons for them (Troy Industries). They offered me another curling iron which I said I really didn't want unless they could explain why the one I had malfunctioned and assure me that the same thing wouldn't happen to a new one. They said I would have to send them the curling iron so that their product safety review company could determine the cause of the malfunction. 

It seems strange to me that since others have had similar issues with their curling irons spanning over several years that they don't already know what the cause of the malfunction might be. I don't trust that they care or will follow through to make sure this product is made safe for the public. I hope you are able to follow through with them to see that this occurs.

Thank you,

[REDACTED]
justification: The incident involved a large electrical spark from a curling iron, but no injury occurred. The likelihood of occurrence is considered possible due to multiple reported instances of similar malfunctions with the same product.

incident_description: This Dryer always has had a warm to hot touch while in use. The longer I had it on the hotter it got. I use the dryer maybe once a week on average.  About a couple weeks ago it started to have a slight burning smell while in use. Last night (10-29-2011) I was drying my daughter's hair and the handle started to smoke and the plastic started to bubble right next to the high low off switch.
justification: The incident involved a burning smell, smoke, and bubbling plastic, but no injury was reported. The likelihood of occurrence is considered possible given the gradual development of symptoms over time.

incident_description:
Use of makeup mirror (day setting) apparently caused my eyes to burn.

After discontinuing use of mirror my eyes ceased to burn after about a day and a half to two days.
justification: The incident caused an injury as evidenced by the report of burning eyes, and it was an unlikely event given its specific cause.

incident_description: I recently bought a fahrenheit Model FHT-125pi hair straightener for my daughter.  She accidentally left in on twice while she went to school.  It stayed on all day and burned the top of her dresser. Granted, it is her fault that she left it on but shouldn't these products be required to have a safety auto shut-off?
justification: The incident resulted in property damage but no injury, and the user accidentally left the straightener on, suggesting an unlikely event.

incident_description:
Received a "Style Elements" Hairdryer model # DW778, 125V-60Hz, 1875w manufactured by Yuyao Dewei Electric Appliance & Motor Company, China. It was purchased from a Big Lots store located in Garner NC in late August 2011.
We noticed that the dryer worked very fast, but it seemed to get hotter much quicker than any of my old dryers ever  did. It gets so intensely hot around the handle, that it burns your hand (no injuries as of yet) and just cannot be held. And to the point, that when trying to remove the styling attachments, we could barely touch those either. In fact, last week I  tried to carefully remove the diffuser, and when it finally popped off, it cracked and can no longer be used. 
It is like this at both the low and high settings.  I've looked for more local or regional contact information, but being that the company is located in China, I haven't been able to find anything that doesn't require me to add the "international translation" package to my computer.
justification: The hairdryer gets intensely hot and can burn hands, but no injuries have occurred yet. The issue seems to be a design or manufacturing flaw.

incident_description: There is a company promoting magnetic headbands in my community. [REDACTED] The product name is Magneblooms and they are sold online at www.lehlashop.com. The headbands gave me a terrible headache when I wore them.
justification: The incident resulted in a headache for the individual wearing the Magneblooms headband, indicating an injury. The likelihood of occurrence is rare as there is only one reported case.

incident_description: I was using this product and it blew up in my hand and burnt my wrist. I called Helen of Troy and I e-mailed them a copy of my wrist that was burned. They didn't seem too concerned about my injury. They said to mail back the curling brush which I did. They had an engineer look over the damage and technically, I did not understand the concept of his answer.
